title: Data and methods
text:
Every number was typed in by hand from the manufacturer’s own published geometry chart, read in a web browser on 21 November 2026. Nothing was scraped, and nothing comes from third-party geometry databases. The text of each chart, as read, is kept in the repository (data/chart-captures/), so any number can be traced back.

24 bikes from 19 brands, chosen to cover current race, all-round, and adventure gravel bikes, including Canadian brands (Norco and Devinci).
Every published size. Where a bike has adjustable geometry (Giant and Liv flip chips, the Cervélo Trail Mixer fork insert), each setting has its own rows.
Units: charts in centimetres (Trek and Cannondale) were converted to millimetres. Cannondale publishes its chart as an image, which was read by eye.
Left out: the Rocky Mountain Solo (not listed on the Canadian site when checked), Kona, Ridley, and Niner (gravel pages would not load), and the Surly Grappler (closer to a mountain bike).

Manufacturers change their charts, sometimes without notice. Check the source before buying anything.

raw = FileAttachment("data/gravel_geometry.csv").csv({typed: true})
sources = Array.from(
  new Map(raw.map(d => [d.bike_id, d])).values(),
  d => ({
    Bike: `${d.brand} ${d.model}`,
    Category: d.category,
    Sizes: raw.filter(r => r.bike_id === d.bike_id && (r.is_default_config === true || r.is_default_config === "TRUE")).length,
    "Tyre clearance": d.tyre_clearance_mm,
    Accessed: d.accessed,
    url: d.source_url,
    Notes: d.notes ?? ""
  })
).sort((a, b) => a.Bike.localeCompare(b.Bike))

















Inputs.table(sources, {
  rows: 30,
  maxHeight: 4000,
  layout: "auto",
  columns: ["Bike", "Category", "Sizes", "Tyre clearance", "Accessed", "url", "Notes"],
  header: {url: "Source"},
  format: {
    url: u => htl.html`<a href="${u}" target="_blank" rel="noopener">chart</a>`,
    Accessed: d => d instanceof Date ? d.toISOString().slice(0, 10) : d,
    Notes: n => htl.html`<span style="white-space: normal; display: inline-block; max-width: 34rem;">${n}</span>`
  }
})

title: Data and methods
text:
Categories
Race, all-round, and adventure are this site’s labels, not the manufacturers’. They follow how each manufacturer describes the bike’s intended use. They are a rough grouping for filtering, and several bikes sit near the edges: the Norco Search, for example, is labelled adventure but is long and low, with a slack head angle.

title: Data and methods
text:
How the data were checked
Geometry charts contain redundant numbers: several measurements can be recalculated from the others. Where a recalculated value disagreed with the published one, the typed number was re-read against the chart. The checks run in R/check_geometry.R.








Check
How
Result




Top tube
effective top tube = reach + stack ÷ tan(seat angle)
Within 12 mm for every size except three OPEN WI.DE. sizes, whose “horizontal” top tube is measured differently from its own reach and stack


Wheelbase
rebuilt from stack, reach, head angle, fork offset, BB drop, and chainstay
Within 10 mm for every size with a published offset


Front centre
published front centre plus chainstay against wheelbase
Within 6 mm except the Santa Cruz Stigmata (about 7 mm short), which probably measures front centre differently


Trail
recalculated against published trail, 72 sizes from 11 bikes
Mean difference −0.9 mm (SD 2.5). Orbea runs about 5 mm higher because its chart assumes a smaller tyre


Size order
stack and reach should not shrink as sizes grow
True for every bike

title: Data and methods
text:
What this site calculates
All lengths are in millimetres, angles in degrees. The bottom bracket (BB) is the origin.
Wheel radius. A 700c rim has a 622 mm bead seat diameter. The tyre’s height is taken as equal to its width, so with the reference 45 mm tyre, R = 311 + 45 = 356 mm. The Salsa Cutthroat uses its stock 29 × 2.25” tyre (about 57 mm).
Trail. With head angle θ and fork offset f:
\[\text{trail} = \frac{R \cos\theta - f}{\sin\theta}\]
Mechanical trail is trail × sin θ: the same gap measured at right angles to the steering axis, which is the lever arm the rider actually feels. Wheel flop is trail × sin θ × cos θ: how far the front of the bike drops as the bars turn.
Front centre (horizontal, BB to front axle):
\[\text{front centre} = \text{reach} + \frac{\text{stack} - \text{BB drop}}{\tan\theta} + \frac{f}{\sin\theta}\]
Fork offset, where it isn’t published (Canyon, Devinci, and 3T). Rearranging the wheelbase equation gives the offset from the published wheelbase, chainstay, BB drop, stack, reach, and head angle. For the 118 sizes where offset is published, this lands within 2 mm for 115 of them (mean difference 0.0 mm, SD 0.6). These estimates are marked “est.” on the site. The Santa Cruz Stigmata’s offset comes from an FAQ answer (45 mm) that does not fit its chart, so the chart-based estimate (51 to 52 mm) is used instead.
Toe clearance is the straight-line distance from the BB to the front axle, minus the tyre radius, minus a 172.5 mm crank. A typical shoe reaches about 90 to 110 mm ahead of the pedal axle, so smaller figures suggest toe overlap in tight, slow turns.
Stack-to-reach ratio is stack divided by reach.

title: Data and methods
text:
Drawings
Bikes are drawn from the same numbers, to the same scale, with the BB at the origin. Tubes are straight lines between published points, so curved tubes and bent forks are simplified. Where a chart leaves out head tube or seat tube length (only the Factor ELARA), the drawing uses the median relationship across the other bikes (head tube about stack minus 434 mm, seat tube about 0.86 × stack), and says so.

title: Data and methods
text:
Limitations

Manufacturers measure some things differently. Seat tube length and standover in particular have no single definition, so compare them across brands with care.
Reference tyres differ. Published trail and BB height depend on the tyre each manufacturer assumed, and few say which.
Charts change. Values were read on one date and may since have been updated.
No fit advice. Geometry is one part of fit. A bike’s stem, spacers, bars, and saddle setup change the rider’s position as much as the frame does.

title: Data and methods
text:
Spotted a mistake?
Please open an issue on GitHub with the bike, size, and the number that looks wrong.

title: Explore the bikes
Explore the bikes
text:
What the columns mean


Stack/reach

Stack divided by reach. Higher means a more upright riding position.

Head angle

How steeply the steering axis is tilted. Slacker (lower) angles feel calmer at speed. Steeper (higher) angles feel quicker to turn.

Seat angle

How far forward the saddle sits over the pedals. Steeper angles put you further forward.

Fork offset

How far the fork pushes the front axle ahead of the steering axis. Three brands don’t publish it, so it’s worked back from the wheelbase. Checked against bikes that do publish it, that method lands within 2 mm for 115 of 118 sizes.

Trail

The gap on the ground between where the steering axis points and where the tyre touches down, calculated for a 700 × 45 mm tyre. More trail means steadier, self-centring steering. Gravel bikes mostly sit between 60 and 80 mm.

Wheelbase

The distance between the axles. Longer is steadier, shorter is nimbler.

Chainstay

The distance from the pedals’ axle to the rear axle. Shorter feels livelier. Longer is steadier and leaves more room for tyres.

BB drop

How far the pedals’ axle sits below the wheel axles. More drop puts you lower between the wheels, which feels planted.

Toe clearance

The gap between the pedal axle (crank pointing forward, 172.5 mm cranks) and the front tyre. A shoe usually reaches 90 to 110 mm ahead of the pedal axle, so smaller figures suggest your toe could touch the tyre in tight, slow turns.

Tyre clearance

The widest tyre the manufacturer says fits, in their own words in the data file.

title: Gravel bike geometry. Compared, explained, and test-ridden on paper.
text:
Portfolio project · Quarto · Observable JS · D3


Published geometry for current gravel bikes, every size, typed in from the manufacturers’ own charts and checked against itself. More is on the way: drawings to scale, a rider on each bike, and a custom bike builder.
Explore the bikes Code on GitHub

title: Gravel bike geometry. Compared, explained, and test-ridden on paper.
text:
What this is
A bike’s geometry is the set of lengths and angles that decide how it fits and how it handles. Manufacturers publish them in charts that are hard to compare by eye. This site puts them side by side.

Every number comes from the manufacturer’s own chart, with the page and the date it was read. Charts change, so check the source before buying anything.
The numbers are checked against each other. Trail, top tube, and wheelbase can each be recalculated from the other measurements, which catches typing slips.
No rankings. Different geometry suits different riders and rides. The point is to see the differences, not to pick a winner.

title: Gravel bike geometry. Compared, explained, and test-ridden on paper.
Compare bikes
text:
Pick up to three bikes and a size for each. The table lines up their numbers, shows how each one differs from bike A, and places all three among every size of every bike in the dataset.
raw = FileAttachment("data/gravel_geometry_derived.csv").csv({typed: true})

bikes = raw.map(d => ({
  ...d,
  is_default_config: d.is_default_config === true || d.is_default_config === "TRUE",
  offset_estimated: d.offset_estimated === true || d.offset_estimated === "TRUE",
  size_label: String(d.size_label),
  label: `${d.brand} ${d.model}`
}))

bikeList = Array.from(new Set(bikes.map(d => d.label))).sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b))

slotColours = ({A: "#2563a8", B: "#d2691e", C: "#2a9d8f"})
categoryNames = ({"race": "Race", "all-round": "All-round", "adventure": "Adventure"})

configsFor = bike => Array.from(new Set(bikes.filter(d => d.label === bike).map(d => d.config)))
defaultConfigFor = bike => (bikes.find(d => d.label === bike && d.is_default_config) ?? {}).config
sizesFor = (bike, config) => bikes
  .filter(d => d.label === bike && d.config === config)
  .sort((a, b) => a.size_order - b.size_order)
  .map(d => d.size_label)
// middle size, rounding up, as a sensible starting point
middleSize = sizes => sizes[Math.floor(sizes.length / 2)]
rowFor = (bike, config, size) => bikes.find(d => d.label === bike && d.config === config && d.size_label === size)

// Starting picks: one race, one adventure, one all-round bike
starts = ({
  A: {bike: "Specialized Crux 5", size: "56"},
  B: {bike: "Norco Search C Gen 3", size: "3"},
  C: {bike: "Trek Checkpoint SL Gen 3", size: "ML"}
})
picks = [
  {slot: "A", row: rowFor(bikeA, configA, sizeA)},
  {slot: "B", row: rowFor(bikeB, configB, sizeB)},
  ...(bikeC === "(none)" ? [] : [{slot: "C", row: rowFor(bikeC, configC, sizeC)}])
].filter(p => p.row)

// Everything we compare, grouped, with a plain-language reading of "higher"
measures = [
  {group: "Fit", key: "stack", label: "Stack", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "taller front end, more upright"},
  {group: "Fit", key: "reach", label: "Reach", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "longer front end, more stretched out"},
  {group: "Fit", key: "stack_reach_ratio", label: "Stack/reach", unit: "", dp: 2, higher: "more upright overall"},
  {group: "Fit", key: "head_tube_length", label: "Head tube", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "higher handlebars before spacers"},
  {group: "Fit", key: "seat_tube_angle", label: "Seat angle", unit: "°", dp: 1, higher: "saddle further forward over the pedals"},
  {group: "Fit", key: "top_tube_effective", label: "Top tube (effective)", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "longer cockpit"},
  {group: "Fit", key: "standover", label: "Standover", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "less room over the top tube (measured differently by each brand)"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "head_tube_angle", label: "Head angle", unit: "°", dp: 1, higher: "steeper, quicker steering"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "fork_offset_used", label: "Fork offset", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "less trail for the same head angle"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "trail_calc", label: "Trail (700 × 45)", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "steadier, more self-centring steering"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "wheelbase", label: "Wheelbase", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "more stable, less nimble"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "front_centre_calc", label: "Front centre", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "front wheel further ahead of the pedals"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "chainstay", label: "Chainstay", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "steadier rear end, more tyre room"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "bb_drop", label: "BB drop", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "pedals sit lower between the wheels"},
  {group: "Handling", key: "toe_clearance", label: "Toe clearance", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "less chance of toe overlap"},
  {group: "Tyres", key: "tyre_clearance_mm", label: "Max tyre width", unit: "mm", dp: 0, higher: "room for wider tyres"}
]

// Reference population for the strips: every size, default setting only
population = bikes.filter(d => d.is_default_config)
legend = html`<div class="gg-legend">${picks.map(p => html`<span><span class="slot-dot" style="background:${slotColours[p.slot]}">${p.slot}</span>${p.row.label}, size ${p.row.size_label}${p.row.config === "standard" ? "" : ` (${p.row.config})`} · ${categoryNames[p.row.category]}</span>`)}</div>`
